How I Did It: City Defense

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Missile Command showed up in my arcade in 1980 with that trackball that felt like it belonged on a boat, not a game cabinet. I remember a fella — grown man, tie and everything, must've just gotten off work downtown — who'd come in on his lunch break and just stand there grim-faced, defending his six little cities like it was personal. Never said a word to anybody. Just fed it quarters, lost all six cities, sighed, and went back to the office. Same time, every day, for about a year.

What the remodel changed

This one used to just check "is the enemy missile close to my explosion" once a tick and call it good, which meant fast missiles could sometimes slip past a blossom that was still very much there, just between checks. Now the explosion's real size gets checked every single moment it's growing and shrinking, not just at a few fixed points, so a warhead that wanders into it at any instant is caught fair and square. I also finally got the chain reactions working right — shoot down a missile that's mid-split and both halves still count, still go boom, still shake the screen. And the crosshair follows your mouse or your finger now instead of a trackball I don't have to clean cigarette tar out of anymore. Small mercies.

The spell that did it

Build Missile Command against our shared engine. Six cities, three missile batteries with ten interceptors each, ammo shown as little stacked pips. The crosshair follows the mouse or touch point, and clicking fires one interceptor from whichever battery is nearest and still has ammo — fast from the center battery, slower from the sides, like the original. Explosions should expand then shrink and catch anything that flies into them, including chain reactions. Give me MIRVs that split, smart bombs that dodge unless you catch them dead center, and the occasional bomber flying across. Wave clears should tally a bonus with some nice tick sounds, and losing all six cities ends it with THE END in big letters, just like I remember it.

Under the hood

  • Same fixed-timestep trick as the other games — the blossom radius grows and shrinks on a clock, not a frame count, so it looks the same on every machine.
  • A warhead that gets caught mid-flight throws its own smaller blossom, and that one can catch the next missile over — that's the "chain reaction" the original was famous for, and it just kind of works once you write the collision check once and let it run on every explosion, old or new.
  • The bonus tally at the end of a wave isn't just adding a number — it ticks the score up bit by bit with a little coin sound, same as standing there watching the real machine count your leftover ammo.
  • Every ten thousand points rebuilds one ruined city, if you've got one to rebuild. That part always felt like the game giving you a little mercy, and I wanted to keep that feeling exactly.
